titre: The Objection That Stalled Copernicus for Three Centuries
accroche: If the Earth orbits the Sun, the stars should wobble. It took 295 years to see the wobble
contenu_vulgarise:
Hold a finger out in front of you and close each eye in turn. The finger jumps against the background of the room. The farther you move it, the less it jumps.

This apparent shift has a name, parallax, and it supplies a formidable argument against Copernicus.

If the Earth really travels in an orbit around the Sun, then in January and July it occupies two positions three hundred million kilometers apart. These are two eyes set very wide. Nearby stars should therefore wobble against the more distant stars over the course of the year.

Nobody saw anything.

## Two ways out, and only one was true

The absence of a wobble allows two readings. Either the Earth does not move. That was the position of Tycho Brahe, who was no fool. Or the stars are so far away that the wobble falls below what we know how to measure.

The second requires accepting distances no one had imagined. Copernicus himself had to resign himself to it, and it passed for a convenient escape hatch.

Settling the question meant measuring a tiny angle, on a well-chosen star, with an instrument of unprecedented precision.

## How Bessel won the race

In 1838, Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel pulls it off. His choice of target does half the work.

He does not aim at a bright star. Brightness depends as much on intrinsic power as on distance, and can fool you. He aims at 61 Cygni, a faint star but one whose proper motion across the sky is very fast. And a high proper motion is the sign of a nearby object.

Over six months he measures a shift on the order of a third of an arcsecond. That is the angle at which you would see a coin from several kilometers away.

The distance he derives from it is about ten light-years.

## What the number settled

At a stroke, two things fall.

First, the anti-Copernican objection: the wobble exists, it was simply too small. The Earth's motion stops being a convenient hypothesis and becomes a measured fact, 295 years after Copernicus's publication.

And then, the scale of the world. The stars are not a little farther away than the planets. They are hundreds of thousands of times farther. The void between the stars becomes the principal substance of the universe.

The case deserves to be kept in mind whenever a theory predicts an effect that is not observed. Seeing nothing does not refute; it measures the sensitivity of the instrument. But you still have to know which of the two readings you are holding, and only a better instrument can tell you that.

repere.texte: In 1838, Bessel measures a shift of about a third of an arcsecond for 61 Cygni, corresponding to a distance of roughly ten light-years. Copernicus had published 295 years earlier.
repere.source: Karl M. Menten, “The Distances of the Stars,” Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy

carte.punch: Observing nothing does not refute a theory. It measures your instrument.
carte.idee: If the Earth orbits, nearby stars should wobble in the sky. Nobody saw anything, and the argument was used against Copernicus. Bessel measures the wobble in 1838: about a third of an arcsecond, or roughly ten light-years.

quiz.question: Why did the absence of stellar parallax trouble Copernicus's model?
choix: Because it implied that the stars revolved around the Earth
Because it made any calculation of the distance to the Sun impossible
Because an orbiting Earth should make nearby stars wobble
Because it contradicted the position measurements made by Tycho Brahe
quiz.explication: Two positions of the Earth six months apart make two very distant points of view: nearby stars should appear displaced against the background. Seeing nothing left two ways out: the Earth is motionless, or the stars are far more distant than anyone imagined. Bessel settled it by finally measuring the angle.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who defended the position that the Earth does not move, a position the card does not present as that of a naive person?
choix: Nicolaus Copernicus
Tycho Brahe
Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel
Johannes Kepler
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card specifies that the observed absence of a wobble could be explained either by an immobile Earth, the position defended by Tycho Brahe, who was no fool, or by stars too distant for the effect to be measurable.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Bessel choose to aim at the star 61 Cygni rather than a brighter star?
choix: Because it was the easiest to spot with the naked eye from the observatory
Because it had already been successfully measured by Copernicus himself
Because it lay exactly opposite the Sun in every season
Because its very fast proper motion across the sky is the sign of a nearby object
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card explains that a star's brightness can fool you, because it depends as much on its intrinsic power as on its distance: Bessel therefore aims at 61 Cygni for its very fast proper motion, the sign of a nearby object.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the card compare the size of the angle Bessel measured, about a third of an arcsecond, to?
choix: The angle at which you would see a coin from several kilometers away
The angle at which you would see the Moon from the Earth
The thickness of a hair seen from one meter away
The angle a watch hand sweeps in one second
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card gives this image to convey how tiny the measured angle is, a third of an arcsecond: it is the angle at which you would see a coin from several kilometers away.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the card, what does Bessel's result settle in addition to the anti-Copernican objection?
choix: The exact number of planets in the solar system
The chemical composition of nearby stars
The scale of the world, with the stars far beyond the planets
The speed at which the Earth rotates on its axis
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card indicates that two things fall at once with Bessel's measurement: the anti-Copernican objection, and the scale of the world, since the stars turn out to be hundreds of thousands of times farther away than the planets.
